title: LOK SABHA SPEAKER CALLS FOR A PEOPLE’S MOVEMENT TO MAKE YAMUNA CLEAN AND ENSURE ITS UNINTERRUPTED FLOW
subtitle:
INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT MUST NOT COME AT THE COST OF ENVIRONMENT; SCIENTIFIC TREATMENT OF SEWAGE AND INDUSTRIAL WASTE ESSENTIAL: LOK SABHA SPEAKER

LOK SABHA SPEAKER SAYS RIVER CONSERVATION IS A COLLECTIVE MORAL RESPONSIBILITY AND VITAL TO SAFEGUARDING FUTURE GENERATIONS

ENVIRONMENT-FRIENDLY LIFESTYLES AND PUBLIC PARTICIPATION KEY TO PROTECTING RIVERS AND WATER RESOURCES: LOK SABHA SPEAKER

LOK SABHA SPEAKER PARTICIPATES IN NATIONAL CAMPAIGN FOR YAMUNA CONSERVATION; ADMINISTERS SANKALP TO PARTICIPANTS TO MAKE THE RIVER CLEAN
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                22 NOV 2026 10:37PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Lok Sabha Speaker Shri Om Birla today called for a sustained people’s movement to make the river Yamuna clean and ensure its uninterrupted flow. Emphasising that government efforts must be supported by active public participation, he urged citizens, institutions, industry and social organisations to make river conservation a shared responsibility.
Shri Birla made these observations while addressing the National Campaign of Conservation and Public Resolution for River Maa Yamuna Ji at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi today. On the occasion, the Speaker also administered a Sankalp to the invitees to make  Yamuna clean and called upon everyone to contribute to fulfilling this collective resolve.
Highlighting the importance of rivers in India’s civilisational journey, Shri Birla observed that rivers have sustained human settlements, agriculture, industry and livelihoods for generations. The Ganga and the Yamuna, he said, are integral to India’s spiritual and cultural heritage, and their conservation is essential to protecting both this legacy and the well-being of society. He emphasised that preserving India’s traditions and values must also involve safeguarding its rivers and natural environment.
Shri Birla stressed that every member of society must act responsibly to preserve the cleanliness and sanctity of the Yamuna. Keeping riverbanks clean and ensuring that everyday conduct does not contribute to pollution, he said, must become a collective moral responsibility. He observed that conservation efforts gain strength and achieve lasting results when they become a Jan Andolan supported by all sections of society.
Calling upon industry to contribute actively to river conservation, Shri Birla said that industries are an important foundation of development, but their growth must not come at the cost of the environment. He emphasised the need for scientific treatment and effective systems to prevent sewage and industrial waste from entering rivers. Development, environmental protection and water conservation, he noted, must advance together.
Lok Sabha Speaker Speaker underlined the importance of adopting environment-friendly lifestyles, recalling Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s appeal for responsible individual and collective action to protect the environment. He referred to initiatives such as ‘Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam’ and encouraged citizens to participate in efforts that promote greenery, conserve water and reduce environmental degradation. Lasting improvements, he said, require changes in habits and behaviour alongside institutional measures.
Appreciating the efforts of Swami Chidanand Saraswati Ji, Shri Birla said that his work brings together spiritual consciousness and social responsibility to promote environmental protection. He commended his initiatives to mobilise society for river conservation, water conservation and tree plantation, and urged participants to carry forward the resolve to rejuvenate the Yamuna. He also acknowledged the dedication of young volunteers working for the conservation of the Ganga and the Yamuna.
Shri Birla observed that the Yamuna supports the lives and livelihoods of people across several States and called for comprehensive measures for river conservation, prevention of erosion and protection of water resources. He emphasised that sustained community cooperation is indispensable to keeping rivers clean and maintaining their flow. Recalling the relative improvement in river cleanliness during the COVID period, he urged society to reflect on the impact of human activities and accept responsibility for preventing pollution.
Referring to the Yamuna’s special association with Mathura, Vrindavan and the traditions of Lord Shri Krishna, Shri Birla said that the river occupies a deeply cherished place in India’s spiritual consciousness. This sense of reverence, he observed, must translate into practical and sustained action to protect the river wherever it flows.
Emphasising the need to secure a safe future for the coming generations, Shri Birla said that clean rivers and a healthy environment are essential to their well-being. He described climate change as a shared global challenge and observed that India, guided by the philosophy of _Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam,_ has a responsibility to contribute to collective solutions and provide leadership in environmental protection.

title: Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal Chairs Interaction with Tea Industry Stakeholders at Kurseong, Darjeeling
subtitle:
Deliberations Focus on Revitalising Darjeeling Tea, Strengthening Tea Auctions and Enhancing Exports

India Remains the World’s Largest Producer of Black Tea and Third-Largest Exporter, Recording USD 988.13 Million in Tea Exports in FY 2025–26
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                22 NOV 2026 10:08PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of Commerce and Industry, Shri Piyush Goyal, chaired an interaction with tea industry stakeholders at Kurseong, West Bengal, organised by Tea Board India. The meeting was also attended by Member of Parliament, Darjeeling, Shri Raju Bista, and MLA, Kurseong, Shri Sonam Lama.
Senior officials of the State Government, representatives of various tea associations and stakeholders from different segments of the Indian tea industry participated in the interaction. The meeting provided an important platform for constructive dialogue on key challenges, emerging opportunities and measures required to strengthen the long-term growth, sustainability and global competitiveness of the Indian tea sector.
India continues to be the world's largest producer of black tea and the third-largest exporter of tea globally. During the financial year 2025–26, India exported 282.11 million kg of tea, valued at USD 988.13 million, underscoring the sector's significant contribution to the country's agricultural economy and export earnings.
Detailed deliberations were held on a wide range of issues, including the revitalisation of the Darjeeling tea industry, making the tea auction system more responsive, faster and robust, strengthening tea research, quality enhancement, export promotion, welfare of tea workers and initiatives under the Export Promotion Mission (EPM).
An extensive brainstorming session was also held on making the existing tea auction system more robust, efficient, faster and responsive to the evolving requirements of the industry. The importance of technology-driven reforms, greater transparency, improved operational efficiency and reduction of transaction-related difficulties was highlighted.
Ease of Doing Business emerged as a key priority, with emphasis on simplifying processes, improving efficiency and creating a more enabling environment for stakeholders across the tea value chain.
Considerable emphasis was placed on strengthening Indian tea exports through focused promotional measures and effective utilisation of opportunities under the Government of India's Export Promotion Mission. Stakeholders shared suggestions for expanding India's presence in international markets, strengthening the global positioning of Indian tea, improving market access and enhancing export competitiveness. Discussions also highlighted the need for coordinated efforts between the Government, Tea Board India and industry stakeholders to promote Indian tea in both traditional and emerging markets.
The critical role of research and development in improving the quality, productivity and competitiveness of Indian tea was emphasised during the interaction. Discussions focused on strengthening tea research, encouraging innovation and adopting improved scientific practices to address emerging challenges and meet the evolving quality requirements of domestic and international markets. The services of the Tea Research will be extended to small tea growers.
The welfare of tea plantation workers and their families remained an important area of discussion. In this context, reference was made to the proposed implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Cha Shramik Protsahan Yojana (PMCSPY), aimed at improving the welfare of tea workers, particularly women and their children, in West Bengal. The significance of effective implementation of the scheme and its intended benefits in the areas of education, healthcare and improved living conditions was highlighted.
The interaction provided an opportunity for stakeholders to present their concerns, share suggestions and deliberate on practical measures for the overall development of the tea sector. The discussions underscored the importance of a coordinated approach towards revitalising the Darjeeling tea industry, modernising tea trading infrastructure, promoting Ease of Doing Business, strengthening research and quality assurance, enhancing exports, improving the welfare of tea workers and strengthening the tea auction system.

Union Home and Cooperation Minister launches major development projects worth ₹5,610.95 crore, flags off mobile medical vans and inaugurates the SARAS Mela
date:

                22 NOV 2026 6:06PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Taking an important step towards strengthening the cooperative movement in the country and making it a powerful instrument of self-reliance and public welfare, a Cooperative Festival was organised today in Itanagar, the capital of Arunachal Pradesh, under the vision of ‘Sahkar Se Samriddhi’ of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi and the guidance of Union Home and Cooperation Minister Shri Amit Shah. Shri Amit Shah attended the event at the Dorjee Khandu State Convention Centre, unveiled the ‘Arunachal Pradesh Cooperative Vision 2047’ and launched various development projects for the State. Several important initiatives were undertaken to promote cooperative institutions, strengthen rural livelihoods, connect women’s Self-Help Groups with markets and accelerate the overall development of the State. Chief Minister of Arunachal Pradesh Shri Pema Khandu, Union Minister for Parliamentary Affairs and Minority Affairs Shri Kiren Rijiju, Deputy Chief Minister of Arunachal Pradesh Shri Chowna Mein, State Home Minister Shri Mama Natung, Cooperation Minister Shri Ojing Tasing, Agriculture Minister Shri Gabriel Denwang Wangsu, Rajya Sabha MP Shri Tai Tagak, sitting MLA from Itanagar Shri Techi Kaso, officials of the Ministry of Cooperation and representatives associated with the cooperative sector of the State were present on the occasion.
Addressing the gathering, Union Home and Cooperation Minister Shri Amit Shah paid his respects to the sacred land of Arunachal Pradesh and said that it is the blessed land where the Sun God first arrives in the country. Arunachal Pradesh is known across India for two special reasons: its ancient tradition of Sun worship and its religious and mythological association with Lord Parshuram. He said that the connection between Gujarat and Arunachal Pradesh is also around 6,000 years old. Lord Shri Krishna married Mata Rukmini, who is believed to have been associated with Arunachal Pradesh and later settled in Dwarka. Appreciating the extraordinary natural wealth and beauty of Arunachal Pradesh, Shri Shah, who hails from Gujarat, said that whenever he visits the State, the company of nature relieves him of all the fatigue and stress of Delhi politics.
Shri Amit Shah said that over the last 12 years, under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, unprecedented priority has been accorded to the development and connectivity of the Northeast. Today, there is no State in the Northeast whose capital is not connected by rail and air services. Historic efforts have been made to connect the Northeast with the rest of the country through roads, railways, air services and now waterways. He said that the Northeast has received its greatest connectivity boost during the tenure of the present Central Government in the nearly eight decades since Independence. Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi has not only reduced the physical distance between Delhi and the Northeast but has also bridged the emotional distance between them. He has personally promoted educational opportunities, skill development and employment prospects for the youth of the Northeast, while also highlighting the region’s tourism potential across the country. Shri Shah said that the Prime Minister has also taken steps to promote industrial development in the Northeast in a manner that expands economic activity without harming the region’s natural beauty and environment.
The Union Home and Cooperation Minister said that the positive results of these efforts are visible across the Northeast, including Arunachal Pradesh. He stated that before the present Government came to power at the Centre, the budget of Arunachal Pradesh was approximately ₹12,000 crore, which has now increased to ₹36,000 crore. This is an important example of the development achieved by the State over the last 12 years. He also expressed happiness that during his two-day visit to Arunachal Pradesh, he learnt that the Arunachal Pradesh Police had been conferred the President’s Colour. Arunachal Pradesh has become the 17th State in the country to receive this honour for its police force. This achievement is a matter of pride and honour for the entire State.
Shri Amit Shah said that the Central Government has resolved to develop the border villages of the Northeast as the first villages of the country, rather than treating them as the last villages. The Vibrant Villages Programme was launched with this vision. He said that the positive results of the programme are now becoming visible in villages along the China border in Arunachal Pradesh. Earlier, people were migrating from 40 such villages, but now residents have started returning and the population has increased. Facilities relating to electricity, education, healthcare, employment and drinking water have been strengthened in these villages. He said that, to promote the local economy in border villages, the Ministry of Home Affairs has ensured that the ITBP and the Army procure their essential supplies from local villages and their cooperative institutions. As a result, local women are supplying dairy products, eggs, vegetables, millets, flour and other items through cooperative societies. This has strengthened the local agricultural and rural economy while also deepening the emotional bond between residents of border villages and the security forces.
The Union Home and Cooperation Minister said that Arunachal Pradesh has immense potential to make its rural economy self-reliant through the cooperative movement. He called upon the State to become self-reliant in the production of milk, eggs, meat and fish, stating that these products should not have to be sourced from outside the State. If Arunachal Pradesh achieves self-reliance in these four sectors, at least 32,000 families can become economically self-reliant. He said that this goal can be achieved through cooperative societies, fisheries cooperatives and dairy producer cooperatives. The State Government should formulate a well-planned programme for this purpose, and all cooperative institutions and women’s Self-Help Groups should take up this challenge. He assured that the National Cooperative Development Corporation (NCDC) and NABARD would extend full support wherever capital is required for these efforts.
Shri Amit Shah said that more than 56,000 people in Arunachal Pradesh are associated with the cooperative movement through 185 Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), 52 dairy cooperative societies and 43 fisheries cooperative societies. Referring to the State’s water resources and large hydropower dams, he emphasised the need to fully utilise the potential of fisheries cooperatives. He said that large reservoirs and favourable natural conditions could be used to promote cooperative-based fisheries, generating employment for a large number of rural families. Similarly, a comprehensive roadmap should be prepared to expand dairy activities in villages where temperature and climatic conditions are suitable for livestock rearing. He assured that the procurement of milk produced in Arunachal Pradesh would be ensured by Amul and the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB), and efforts would be made to develop milk-processing facilities within the State. He said that the availability of high-quality livestock, formation of cooperative institutions and expansion of animal husbandry would be important steps in this direction. Representatives of NDDB and Amul would soon be sent to Arunachal Pradesh to prepare a district-level roadmap for dairy development. This would economically empower rural women and strengthen family incomes, as well as support the education and well-being of the next generation.
The Union Home and Cooperation Minister said that the overall development of Arunachal Pradesh cannot be assessed merely through economic indicators such as the budget, Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) or GST collection. The true objective of development should be to ensure employment, education, healthcare and family well-being for every person in the State. He said that development should be visible not merely in government documents and statistics, but in the lives of citizens. Happiness on every person’s face, a healthy body, an educated and capable mind, and the commitment to carry forward one’s culture and values are the hallmarks of a developed society. Cooperative institutions should become a means of ensuring economic prosperity for every family. He said that building a developed Arunachal Pradesh is also essential to realising the goal of a developed India.
Referring to the contribution of the Central Government to the development of Arunachal Pradesh, Shri Amit Shah said that the State received ₹33,530 crore from the Central Government between 2004 and 2014, whereas ₹1,49,664 crore was provided between 2014 and 2024 under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, nearly four times the earlier amount. He said that during this period, the devolution fund increased 18 times and grants-in-aid increased by one and a half times. Highlighting infrastructure development in the State, he said that the 1,500-kilometre Frontier Highway has been approved at a cost of ₹44,000 crore. The 2,880 MW Dibang Hydropower Project has been initiated at a cost of ₹32,000 crore. Work has commenced on eight packages covering a total length of 266 kilometres on National Highway-913, at a cost of ₹6,600 crore. The approximately 300-kilometre Balipara–Charduar–Tawang road connecting West Kameng and Tawang districts, the construction of the Nechiphu Tunnel and the bridge over the Sisiri River in Dibang Valley are also important components of this development journey. He said that all three airports at Likabali, Hollongi and Tezu were built during the tenure of the Government led by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. Responding to the Chief Minister’s request for a second daily flight connecting the State with Delhi, he said that discussions had been held with Air India and efforts were underway to introduce a second Itanagar–Delhi flight as new aircraft become available.
The Union Home and Cooperation Minister said that the Central Government has effectively implemented several public welfare schemes to ensure that the benefits of development reach every citizen of the State. More than 1.28 lakh farmers in the State have benefited from the PM-KISAN scheme, tap water connections have been provided to 2.30 lakh households, and 1.90 lakh people are being provided treatment facilities of up to ₹5 lakh under the Ayushman Bharat scheme. In addition, toilets have been constructed in 1.68 lakh households, 8.32 lakh people are being provided five kilograms of foodgrains per person per month, 56,000 gas cylinders have been provided and housing has been made available to approximately 48,000 families. He said that the Central Government is committed to improving the State’s infrastructure and the standard of living of its citizens, and is continuously working to realise Arunachal Pradesh’s potential in all sectors, including tourism.
On the occasion, Union Minister for Parliamentary Affairs and Minority Affairs Shri Kiren Rijiju said that Arunachal Pradesh has the important responsibility of protecting its tribal identity, culture, traditions and land rights, while also ensuring that the next generation has access to better roads, education, healthcare facilities, modern technology and employment opportunities. He said that the State has limited capital and technological resources, and it is necessary to develop a balanced framework to attract large investments while safeguarding the constitutional and land-related rights of local communities and creating new development opportunities. Describing the cooperative movement as an effective means of achieving self-reliance in this direction, he said that cooperative institutions can play an important role in sectors such as agriculture, horticulture and tourism. Shri Rijiju said that since 2014, under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi and the guidance of Shri Amit Shah, Arunachal Pradesh has witnessed significant transformation in roads and infrastructure, national highways and connectivity in border areas. The positive results of the Vibrant Villages Programme have also encouraged people to return to border villages. He expressed confidence that the goal of a developed Arunachal Pradesh, alongside a developed India, could be achieved by 2047, and that the visit of the Union Home and Cooperation Minister would provide a new direction and momentum to the cooperative movement and overall development of the State.
On the occasion, Union Home and Cooperation Minister Shri Amit Shah unveiled the ‘Arunachal Pradesh Cooperative Vision 2047’ and felicitated four cooperative societies for their outstanding performance. The Namsai Dairy Cooperative Society received the ‘Cooperation Excellence Award’; the Lower Subansiri Fish Farmers Cooperative Society was recognised as the Best Fisheries Cooperative Society; Kemli LAMPS received the award for Best Handloom, Textile and Weaver Cooperative Society; and Jang LAMPS was awarded the Best PACS/LAMPS. NCDC presented a loan certificate to Lagun Multipurpose Cooperative Society Limited; the Bharatiya Beej Sahakari Samiti Limited (BBSSL) provided 25 vegetable seed mini-kits; NABARD provided a micro-ATM to Poma Jute Dairy and Livestock Cooperative Society; and the Arunachal Pradesh State Cooperative Apex Bank Limited presented a loan certificate to Wakro LAMPS. A registration certificate was also presented to Khamyer Ane Multipurpose Cooperative Society Limited, formed by a Cluster Level Federation (CLF) of women’s Self-Help Groups.
During the programme, the Union Home and Cooperation Minister launched ‘Mission Shikshit Arunachal – Phase II’, with an outlay of ₹1,500 crore; the ‘Chief Minister’s Comprehensive State Power Development Programme’, worth ₹2,000 crore; and the ‘Chief Minister’s Comprehensive State Rural Road Development Programme’, worth ₹2,000 crore. In addition, 199 projects under the Vibrant Villages Programme in 11 border districts of the State, with an outlay of ₹110.95 crore, and ‘Mission SURAKSHA’ were also launched. Thus, a total outlay of ₹5,610.95 crore has been earmarked for these four major development initiatives. The Union Home and Cooperation Minister also virtually inaugurated a foodgrain storage warehouse at Raga LAMPS under the Grain Storage Scheme and launched an e-commerce webpage for products of the Arunachal State Rural Livelihoods Mission (ArSRLM). These initiatives will strengthen the storage capacity of cooperative institutions, improve market access for rural products and promote the economic activities of women’s Self-Help Groups.
At the beginning of the programme, Union Home and Cooperation Minister Shri Amit Shah flagged off mobile medical vans and inaugurated the SARAS Mela. He visited various stalls at the Mela and interacted with members of women’s Self-Help Groups and cooperative societies. The mobile medical units, flagged off for villages in 11 border districts under the Vibrant Villages Programme, are solar-powered and equipped with facilities such as telemedicine, AI-based portable TB screening, digital X-ray, ECG and modern laboratory services. The SARAS Mela showcased local products, traditional crafts and other items prepared by women’s Self-Help Groups, providing them with direct market access and opportunities to market their products.

title: First SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum Concludes in New Delhi, Reaffirming Shared Heritage and Strengthening Cultural Cooperation Among Member Nations
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                22 NOV 2026 6:12PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The
First Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum
was organised jointly by the Ministry of Culture, and the Ministry of External Affairs, Government of India, with the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) serving as the Knowledge Partner. The Forum was inaugurated by the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India,
Shri Narendra Modi
, on 20 November 2026 at the historic Purana Qila, New Delhi. It brought together 116 delegates from 22 countries, including four Ministers and the Secretary General of the SCO, Mr. Nurlan Yermekbayev. Deputy Ministers, Ambassadors, senior government officials, scholars, subject experts, cultural representatives and officials of the SCO Secretariat were also part of the gathering.
Conceived as a platform for dialogue among the diverse civilisational traditions of the SCO region, the Forum enabled participating countries to reflect on their historical interconnections and consider how these enduring links could inform contemporary cultural cooperation. Across three days, the programme combined high-level deliberations, thematic exchanges, heritage engagements and cultural presentations.
20 November 2026 - Inaugural Session
The inaugural-day programme commenced with a cultural presentation, followed by the screening of a short film on the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum. The programme also featured two exhibitions at Purana Qila. “
ASTITVA - The Essence of Our Existence
” presented the archaeological and cultural layers of Delhi, while the “
Mahabharat Scroll Pavilion
” displayed a rare eighteenth-century illustrated Mahabharata scroll, offering a glimpse into India’s manuscript and artistic heritage.
In his inaugural address, the Hon’ble Prime Minister emphasised that civilisational dialogue can make a meaningful contribution to peace, mutual understanding and trust among nations. He recalled India’s historical cultural connections with Central Asia, China, Southeast Asia and the wider Eurasian region, nurtured through trade, scholarship, spiritual journeys and the movement of ideas and knowledge across the geography.
Drawing attention to the journeys of knowledge across societies, the Prime Minister referred to the Panchatantra, the Ramayana and the transmission of mathematical knowledge, alongside shared influences in music, architecture, spiritual traditions and artistic expression. He invited SCO countries to build on this legacy through contemporary initiatives, including the use of digital technologies and artificial intelligence, digitisation of manuscripts and collections, collaborative research, joint exhibitions, academic exchanges, cultural tourism and greater engagement with young people. His address underscored the relevance of the civilisational ideal of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam in strengthening partnerships across the region.
21 November 2026
The day opened with the thematic session “
Civilisational and Cultural Expressions
”, chaired by the Hon’ble Minister of Culture, Government of India. Ministers and representatives of participating countries presented perspectives on their cultural traditions, historical experiences and areas of common interest. The exchanges brought into focus the importance of safeguarding tangible and intangible heritage, strengthening institutional linkages, encouraging interaction among scholars and artists, and advancing joint research and documentation.
A dedicated session organised by the Archaeological Survey of India, titled “
A Shared Cultural Canvas - Artistic and Architectural Exchanges Among SCO Nations
”, examined the many historical encounters that have shaped the region’s artistic and architectural landscape. Discussions traversed prehistoric and Bronze Age linkages, Buddhist art and architecture, Silk Route exchanges, Indo-Persian influences and maritime connections, while also considering collaborative approaches to heritage conservation and digital documentation.
Delegates, accompanied by the Hon’ble Minister of Culture, visited “
The Light and the Lotus: Relics of the Awakened One
” at the Qila Rai Pithora Cultural Complex. The visit offered an opportunity to engage with India’s Buddhist heritage and the wider Asian networks through which Buddhist thought, art and sacred relic traditions travelled. The day’s programme concluded with a cultural presentation by the Sangeet Natak Akademi, followed by dinner.
22 November 2026
The final day’s deliberations centred on two themes:
“Language, Literature, Script and Manuscript Traditions
” and “
Monastic Trails - Religious and Philosophical Traditions
”. The first session explored approaches to preserving languages, scripts, manuscripts and literary heritage, as well as the transmission of knowledge across generations and geographical boundaries. The second examined the journeys of faith and philosophy and the historical relationships linking religious institutions, centres of learning and communities across the SCO region.
The discussions provided participating countries with an opportunity to identify shared priorities and consider practical avenues for cooperation in preservation, research, documentation, academic engagement and cultural partnerships.
As an outcome of the Forum,
Indraprastha Communiqué
was prepared to capture the principal themes, perspectives and areas of convergence emerging from the three days of deliberations. It reflects the discussions held during the Forum and is intended to provide a useful reference for taking forward continued dialogue and cultural cooperation among SCO countries.
Read the
Indraprastha Communiqué
here
.
At the conclusion of the day’s deliberations, delegates will be taken to the
Red Fort
, a landmark of India’s historical and cultural heritage to be followed by the light-and-sound show (Jai Hind) at the Red Fort, offering delegates an immersive presentation of the monument’s history and its importance in India’s national heritage.
The Forum reaffirmed the value of sustained civilisational engagement as a means of deepening mutual understanding and building enduring relationships among the countries of the SCO. By bringing historical connections into conversation with contemporary opportunities, the gathering provided fresh impetus to cultural cooperation across the region.

title: National Zoological Park organizes  22nd Sunday Bird Walk to Promote Citizen Science and Conservation Awareness; Records 45 Bird Species
ministry: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                22 NOV 2026 10:02PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Zoological Park, New Delhi, organised the 22nd edition of its ‘Sunday Bird Walk @ NZP’ on 22 November 2026, from 7:30 AM to 10:30 AM, reaffirming its commitment to biodiversity documentation, environmental awareness and citizen participation in wildlife conservation.
The nature walk witnessed the participation of 10 nature enthusiasts, students, wildlife photographers and citizens interested in birdwatching and biodiversity. Guided by resource experts and dedicated volunteers, participants explored the avian diversity of the Zoo and learnt about bird identification, behaviour, ecology and their ecological significance.
During the walk, participants documented 45 bird species and more than 400 individual birds in the designated area. The observations contributed to field-based biodiversity documentation and provided participants with an enriching hands-on experience of citizen science. Discussions during the walk highlighted the ecological importance of birds, including their role in natural pest control, maintaining ecological balance and serving as indicators of environmental quality and ecosystem health.
Addressing the participants, the Director (NZP), Dr. Sanjeet Kumar highlighted that citizen science initiatives such as Sunday Bird Walks provide an effective platform to connect people with nature, develop field-identification skills and promote a deeper understanding of ecological relationships and food webs. He emphasised that systematic documentation of biodiversity, supported by public participation, can contribute meaningfully to conservation awareness and environmental stewardship. The Director encouraged nature enthusiasts and citizens to actively participate in such initiatives and become ambassadors for wildlife conservation. The programme concluded with an interactive discussion and feedback session, during which participants shared their observations and experiences, followed by a group photograph.
The National Zoological Park regularly organises Sunday Bird Walks to encourage birdwatching, biodiversity documentation and public engagement in conservation. Each walk is limited to 20–25 participants to ensure meaningful learning and interaction. Prior registration is mandatory, with registrations open from Monday to Friday each week and participation offered on a first-come, first-served basis. The registration link is available on the official website of the National Zoological Park and through the NZP Saathi mobile application.

title: Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava inaugurates Sleep Study Facility and Autism Lab, flags off E-cart Ambulance at IIT Madras
subtitle:
Smt. Srivastava visits key healthcare research and innovation centres at IIT Madras, covering brain research, cancer studies and medical technologies

Indigenous healthcare and assistive technologies at IIT Madras aim to improve access to affordable healthcare and support persons with disabilities and the elderly
ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                22 NOV 2026 8:44PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava today inaugurated the Sleep Study Facility and Autism Lab at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras and flagged off an E-cart Ambulance service at the Institute Hospital. Her visit also included the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre, Department of Medical Sciences and Technology, National Cancer Tissue Biobank, Healthcare Technology Innovation Centre (HTIC) and National Centre for Assistive Health Technologies (NCAHT), covering the Institute's work in healthcare research, medical technologies and assistive solutions.
The newly established Sleep Study Facility at the Campus Health Centre will provide specialised assessment, consultation and treatment for sleep-related disorders among students, faculty, staff and researchers, with support from specialists associated with Kauvery Hospitals, Chennai. Subject to institutional ethics approval and informed consent, it will also enable research on sleep patterns and different types of sleep disorders. The faculty also intends to develop indigenous, cost-effective sensors for sleep monitoring and analysis.
The E-cart Ambulance service, introduced as part of the Institute's campus wellness initiative, will facilitate timely medical assistance and convenient transportation within the campus, particularly for elderly members of the campus community and patients requiring assistance.
The Autism Lab initiative draws on traditional Indian medical knowledge, clinical expertise and technology to study Integrated Varmam Therapy for children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), as part of the activities leading to the establishment of the Centre for Indian Medical Knowledge (CIMK) at IIT Madras. The Institute proposes to collaborate with the Paediatric Neurology team at AIIMS Jodhpur, which has experience in administering the integrated therapy to more than 800 children, to study and scientifically evaluate the treatment protocol. The initiative also envisages developing indigenous pressure sensing gloves to provide real-time feedback to practitioners, alongside research into the possible genetic, molecular and epigenetic mechanisms underlying the therapy, subject to requisite ethical approvals.
At the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre, Smt. Srivastava was informed about its work in developing high-resolution, three-dimensional digital maps of the human brain at cellular resolution. On 11th October 2026, the Hon'ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi dedicated the Centre to the nation and launched its mission to create cellular-resolution maps of over 100 human brains across different stages of life, including brain-related diseases. The Prime Minister also released C-STROKE, the world's first human ischaemic stroke atlas, comprising over 1,000 annotated brain sections.
The Union Health Secretary was then briefed on the interdisciplinary work of the Department of Medical Sciences and Technology, which brings together medical sciences, engineering and technology to address unmet healthcare needs. Established in 2023, the Department focuses on developing physician-scientists and engineering physiologists, with research spanning cardiovascular medicine, neurology, oncology, medical imaging, artificial intelligence in healthcare and medical device development.
At the National Cancer Tissue Biobank, Smt. Srivastava was briefed on the work of this joint initiative of the Department of Science and Technology and IIT Madras, which collects and preserves cancer tissue samples with patients' informed consent for research into cancer biology, diagnosis and treatment. A significant outcome of the Biobank's wider research ecosystem is the Bharat Cancer Genome Atlas, launched in February 2025, which aims to develop an India-specific cancer genomic database to support early diagnosis, targeted therapies and personalised treatment strategies.
Subsequently, Smt. Srivastava was apprised of work at the Healthcare Technology Innovation Centre (HTIC) on affordable and indigenous healthcare technologies, including the Mobile Eye Surgical Unit for cataract surgeries in remote areas, 3nethra for early detection of eye diseases, the Neonatal Transport Unit, iQuant for rapid diagnostic testing and ArtSens for cardiovascular health assessment.
Her visit to the National Centre for Assistive Health Technologies (NCAHT) focused on affordable assistive technologies for persons with disabilities and the elderly, including lightweight wheelchairs, power-assisted mobility devices, swimming pool lifts and walking aids for children with cerebral palsy. Among its key innovations is YD One, an ultra-lightweight active wheelchair designed to enhance independent mobility.
Smt. Srivastava was accompanied by Prof. V. Kamakoti, Director, IIT Madras and Prof. R. Sarathi, Dean (Planning), IIT Madras, during her visit to the facilities.

From 2019 to 2026, Ministry of Home Affairs successfully achieved its target of planting and nurturing more than 8 crore trees
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                22 NOV 2026 6:23PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah inaugurated the campus of 12th Battalion of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) in Itanagar, the capital of Arunachal Pradesh. On the occasion, Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Shri Pema Khandu, Union Minister Shri Kiren Rijiju, Arunachal Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister Shri Chowna Mein, Union Home Secretary Shri Govind Mohan, Intelligence Bureau (IB) Director Dr. Mahesh Dikshit, NDRF Director General Shri Piyush Anand and several other dignitaries were present.
Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that 12th Battalion of  National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) is being officially inaugurated here. Arunachal Pradesh and the entire Northeast are among the regions most vulnerable to natural disasters. All the buildings in this campus have been constructed in accordance with earthquake-resistant standards. The first line of defence against natural disasters begins with the facilities of our 12th  Battalion. This campus will serve as a centre for disaster response not only for Arunachal Pradesh and the entire Northeast but also for several neighbouring regions. Training for the State Disaster Response Forces (SDRFs) of all eight Northeastern states will also be conducted here.
Shri Amit Shah said that an Olympic-size swimming pool and a diving tank have also been constructed here for the training of personnel. This Olympic-size pool will be opened free of charge to all swimming athletes from Itanagar and across Arunachal Pradesh. He said that if any swimmer from the Northeast wins a medal at the 2036 Olympics, the journey towards that achievement will begin from this very pool, as athletes from the Northeast have consistently been at the forefront of winning medals in sports. The Ministry of Home Affairs has successfully achieved its target of planting and nurturing more than 8 crore trees during the period from 2019 to 2026. Shri Amit Shah said that every Central Armed Police Force (CAPF) and the NDRF are actively engaged in the tree plantation drive. These 8 crore trees will certainly serve nature.
Union Home Minister said that the NDRF was constituted in the same year that the Disaster Management Act came into force. However, a fundamental transformation in the country's entire disaster management framework began under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. Earlier, the country's overall approach towards disasters was primarily relief-oriented and reactive. Governments would reach affected areas only after a disaster had struck and engage in reconstruction and repair work after the devastation. Under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, the country has moved towards early warning systems, prevention, mitigation, preparedness, disaster risk reduction and a Zero Casualty approach. We no longer remain passive. As soon as an alert is received through the early warning system, NDRF and SDRF personnel immediately reach out to assist people and carry out effective rescue and relief operations at the disaster site. Even before a disaster strikes, not only citizens but also their livestock are evacuated to safer locations to ensure their safety.
Shri Amit Shah said that between 2014 and 2026, the coordinated efforts of the NDRF, SDRF and all the States have helped save the lives of lakhs of citizens. A comprehensive system has been developed in which not only the NDRF and SDRF personnel, but also everyone from Patwaris to NCC cadets, Scout children and Aapda Mitras working across villages remain prepared to assist people even before a disaster strikes. This provides crucial support in rescue and relief operations. No disaster can be prevented, nor can its impact be effectively mitigated, in the absence of institutional preparedness. Since 2014, the Government of India has established a robust and coordinated system by bringing the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), NDRF, SDRF, the Ministry of Home Affairs and the State machinery together, right down to the Patwari level. This system ensures comprehensive deliberations on policies, their formulation by the Ministry of Home Affairs and their effective implementation by the NDRF, SDRF and State machinery.
Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that NDMA has prepared response protocols and SOPs for dealing with various types of disasters and provided them to the States. Between 2014 and 2026, the operational reach and deployment of NDRF have also expanded significantly. Today, the NDRF is deployed at more than 70 locations across the country. In flood-prone areas, NDRF teams reach the locations even before flooding occurs. With advancements in science and technology, early warnings of cyclones, which were earlier available 24 to 48 hours in advance, can now be issued up to seven days ahead. All citizens are safely evacuated from cyclone-affected areas. Over the past four years, this effective system has helped protect lives and property during several cyclones.
Shri Amit Shah said that during several cyclones in recent years, not a single life was lost. This is a direct outcome of our advance preparedness.  NDRF has so far conducted more than 11,000 operations and saved the lives of over 1.61 lakh people. NDRF has not only carried out rescue operations in India but has also extended its services to several countries, including Japan, Nepal, Türkiye and Sri Lanka, bringing honour to NDRF and the Tricolour. Earlier, whenever a disaster struck India, disaster response agencies from across the world would come forward to assist the country. Today, whenever a disaster strikes anywhere in the world, our NDRF proudly represents India and reaches the affected areas to save lives. This is a significant achievement of the Government of India.
The Ministry of Home Affairs has paid special attention to three key areas concerning the NDRF: expansion, resources and training. Resources do not merely mean budgetary allocations; the Ministry has also played an important role in ensuring the availability of modern equipment. The year 2026 has been declared the Year of Capacity Building for the National Disaster Response Force.
Shri Amit Shah said that soon NDRF would have emerged as a leading disaster response force among all such agencies across the world. Northeast India is an extremely important part of our country. It shares borders with several countries and plays a crucial role in many important national initiatives. Today, an NDRF battalion has been established near Itanagar in the border region of Arunachal Pradesh. Our NDRF personnel will be capable of protecting the entire Northeast from disasters, demonstrating their valour and ensuring positive outcomes. The Central Government will extend all possible assistance to the entire Northeastern region, and round-the-clock operations will be conducted throughout the year to save the lives of thousands and lakhs of people in the region.

The timeless appeal of Indian mythology found a global platform on Day 3 of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), as Nitesh Tiwari’s much-awaited epic,
Ramayana: Rise of a Legend (Part 1)
, premiered as the official opening film of the ‘Films from BRICS’ section.
Rooted in one of India’s most enduring epics, the film brings a story that has travelled across generations and cultures to an international cinematic platform. Its selection as the opening film sets the tone for a showcase that celebrates the power of cinema to connect people beyond geographical and linguistic boundaries.
The inaugural segment also featured the felicitation of diplomatic representatives from participating countries. Mr. Saidu Dahiru Muhammed, Ambassador, High Commission of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, was felicitated by Shri Prabhat, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. Ms. Erny Wahyuni, representing the Chargé d’Affaires of the Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia, and Mr. Aleksandr Fursov, Acting Consul General, Consulate General of the Russian Federation in Mumbai, were felicitated by Shri Shambhu Lingappa Hakki, Joint Secretary, Ministry of External Affairs.
Dr. Mostafa Goharifar, Deputy Chief of Mission of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and Dr. Omid Babelian, IPIS Representative in India, were felicitated by Shri G. Krishnakumar, Chairman, National Film Development Corporation (NFDC).
Ms. Meiliza Karunia Harahap, Treasury, Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia, was also felicitated by Shri G. Krishnakumar. Festival Director Shri Ashutosh Gowariker felicitated director Nitesh Tiwari in recognition of his film,
Ramayana: Rise of a Legend (Part 1)
, which opened the ‘Films from BRICS’ section.
The ‘Films from BRICS’ showcase recognises the importance of cinema beyond entertainment. Films offer a window into the lives, values, traditions and aspirations of different societies. They allow countries to present their own perspectives while helping audiences understand cultures beyond their borders. In this context, the BRICS platform provides an opportunity to strengthen people-to-people connections, encourage creative collaboration and give greater visibility to cinematic voices from the Global South.
Together, these films make the ‘Films from BRICS’ section a celebration of cultural diversity and shared human experiences. By bringing stories from different parts of the world to one screen, IFFI reinforces cinema’s role in fostering mutual respect, strengthening cultural ties and building a deeper understanding among nations. The showcase reflects the spirit of
Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam
, or ‘the world is one family’, and underlines how storytelling can bring people closer, even when their languages, histories and traditions differ.
Stories Without Borders: Celebrating Cultural Diversity in the ‘Films from BRICS’ Lineup
Spanning 11-member countries and 10 partner nations, the ‘Films from BRICS’ showcase at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) brings together a diverse range of contemporary storytelling across genres, languages and lived realities. From sweeping mythological spectacle and animated historical reimaginings, such as Nitesh Tiwari’s
Ramayana: Rise of a Legend (Part 1)
and Brenda Lígia and Edu Felistoque’s
Amadeo and the Hypothetical New World

1982

9 Temples to Heaven
, Andrei Egorov’s
And the Snow was Falling

Baab

, Luis Ernesto Donas’s
Baracoa
, Anastasia Kuzina’s
Bo Bo
, Rashid Malikov’s
Cotton
and Katrine Weber’s
Dreaming of Serenada
, these films explore themes of family memory, social pressures, resilience and ecological belonging.
United under this year’s theme, ‘Stories Without Borders’, the lineup highlights how cinema from across BRICS orbit captures distinct cultural identities while speaking to universal human emotions.

title: Film Industry Veterans Discuss the Role of Film Schools at 57th IFFI
subtitle:
Experts underline the importance of institutional training, practical exposure, discipline and adaptability in shaping the next generation of filmmakers

Filmmaking demands continuous practice, experience and exposure to cinema from across the world: Artur Daborski
content:
Goa, 22 November 2026
Can cinema be taught, or must it be discovered? This question set the tone for a panel discussion titled ‘
The Unteachable Frame: Can Cinema Be Taught or Must It Be Discovered?
’ held alongside film screenings at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa today. The discussion explored the role of film schools in nurturing creative talent, imparting technical skills and preparing aspiring filmmakers for the demands of the industry.
The panel featured Amala Akkineni, actor and director of Annapurna College of Film and Media; Anupam Kher, actor and founder of Actor Prepares; Artur Daborski, cultural journalist, vice-rector for international cooperation at Warsaw Film School, programme director of the Summer Film Academy, programmer at the Tofifest International Film Festival and FIPRESCI member; Bhupendra Kainthola, former director of the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII); and Manoj Paramahamsa, cinematographer in the Tamil, Telugu and Malayalam film industries, mentor and founder of Cinema Factory Academy. The session was moderated by Vikramjit Roy, who has held leadership positions at Sony Pictures India and the National Film Development Corporation (NFDC).
Amala Akkineni highlighted the collaborative nature of filmmaking, noting that film schools provide an environment where students learn to work together and understand the interdependence of different filmmaking disciplines. She also called upon film educators to challenge prevailing stereotypes and encourage more women to pursue professional training in filmmaking. Emphasising the importance of commitment, she urged aspiring filmmakers to develop the willingness to go the extra mile.
Sharing his personal experience, Anupam Kher underscored the importance of formal training in shaping an actor’s abilities. Recalling his years at the National School of Drama (NSD), he said, “I would not have been sitting here had I not gone to National School of Drama.”
Referring to his debut film
Saaransh
, in which he portrayed a 65-year-old man at the age of 28, Kher credited his NSD training with equipping him to undertake the challenging role. He identified observation, imagination and emotional memory as three essential qualities of an actor. An individual’s experiences, he explained, are stored in memory and become an important resource for portraying characters convincingly.
Describing acting as an engagement with the nine emotions or
Navarasas
, he said an actor must be able to recall and express them in keeping with the demands of a scene, sequence or story. Film schools help aspiring actors understand, practise and communicate these emotions effectively. Advising young actors to draw inspiration from everyday life, he said, “Every experience teaches you something. What you learn as a human being will help you in your acting.”
Kher also cautioned young actors against complacency, observing that competence can sometimes become an obstacle to brilliance. Artists, he said, must continually strive to improve their skills and craft.
Artur Daborski emphasised that filmmaking demands continuous practice, experience and exposure to cinema from across the world. He highlighted the role of film festivals in introducing young filmmakers to diverse cinematic traditions and enabling them to engage with films and professionals from different backgrounds. Understanding developments in world cinema, he observed, is essential for filmmakers seeking to create something original.
Sharing the approach followed at Warsaw Film School, Daborski said students are encouraged to make films in a supportive institutional environment that allows them to experiment and learn from their mistakes. Such opportunities are important, he noted, as mistakes on professional film sets can have significant financial and practical consequences.
He also stressed the need to prepare students for the business aspects of filmmaking, including pitching projects to producers, securing funding and understanding the professional ecosystem. Exposure to film festivals, he added, is an integral part of this preparation.
Speaking about the kind of films that European festivals look for, Daborski encouraged young filmmakers to explore subjects that trouble them or issues they find difficult to accept. He noted that festivals value films that engage meaningfully with important social and human concerns.
Bhupendra Kainthola highlighted the relationship between artistic expression and institutional training. “Art can be discovered, but craft has to be taught,” he said, emphasising the value of formal education for aspiring film professionals.
He observed that success in filmmaking requires creativity to be supported by discipline, structured learning and adherence to professional processes. Drawing on his experience at FTII, Kainthola noted that many students choose film education despite conventional career expectations within their families. Public-funded institutions such as FTII, he said, have a responsibility to provide an enabling environment in which their creative ambitions can be nurtured.
Manoj Paramahamsa emphasised that professional film sets operate under multiple practical constraints, leaving limited scope for beginners to experiment and learn through trial and error.
Film schools, therefore, provide an important foundation by teaching the fundamentals of filmmaking in a structured environment. Beyond technical skills, they equip students to manage human resources, coordinate teams and work collaboratively, all of which are critical to the successful execution of a film project, he said.
The panel also discussed the growing influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on film education and filmmaking.
Manoj Paramahamsa observed that AI is increasingly being used to simplify repetitive tasks, generate preliminary storyboards and improve production workflows. Technological advances have also transformed visual production, enabling filmmakers to modify backgrounds and create sophisticated visual environments even after filming.
While acknowledging the need to adapt to technological advancements, Anupam Kher emphasised that human emotion remains central to creative expression. Referring to AI-generated virtual avatars, he said technology may be able to create images and performances, but it cannot replicate the heart and soul that human beings bring to acting.
The discussion underscored the continuing relevance of film schools in nurturing creative talent through a combination of institutional training, practical exposure and experimentation. It also highlighted the need for aspiring filmmakers to remain adaptable, technologically aware and committed to continuous learning and reinvention.
The 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), being held in Goa from November 20 to 28, 2026, brings together filmmakers, industry professionals and cinema enthusiasts from India and across the world. Through film screenings, masterclasses and interactive discussions, the festival provides a platform for cinematic exchange, learning and collaboration.

title: “Thousands of Years of Lived Experiences Nourished by the Ganga”: Bharat Bala and A.R. Rahman Reunite for Banaras at IFFI 2026
subtitle:
An intimate father-daughter drama of music, memory and legacy, set on the banks of the Ganges, has its India Premiere in the Indian Panorama section

Beyond the Familiar: Rahman Turns to Lesser-Used Ragas Like Dev Gandharva for Banaras
content:
Goa, 22 November 2026
Filmmaker Bharat Bala reunites with music maestro A.R. Rahman for Banaras, a father-daughter drama selected for the Indian Panorama section of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, where it will have its India premiere. The film features Abhishek Banerjee, Shahana Goswami, Neeraj Kabi, Chhaya Kadam, Indira Tiwari and Antonythasan Jesuthasan, among others.
Set against the cultural and musical landscape of Indian classical music, Banaras explores the relationship between a father and daughter, the inheritance of musical legacy and the enduring bonds between generations. The story unfolds against what director Bharat Bala describes as “the eternal spirit of the Ganges”.
Speaking about the film’s music, A.R. Rahman said that Indian classical music, both Hindustani and Carnatic, has been a constant source of inspiration throughout his creative journey. The ragas and the emotions associated with them, he said, continue to shape his musical expression.
Elaborating on his approach to the film’s score, Rahman spoke about incorporating ragas into its compositions. Reflecting on India’s cultural diversity, Rahman said it continues to inspire his musical exploration. “I enjoy every culture,” he said, noting that every language has its distinct flavour, from the potency of Punjabi to the sweetness of Bengali. He often allows languages and their cultural essence to intermingle in his music.
Bharat Bala spoke about returning to feature filmmaking after a long gap since Maryan, noting that he had worked on several short films in the intervening years. For him, making a feature film is a continuation of the creative process, undertaken when he encounters a story that he feels needs to be told.
While Banaras has been portrayed on screen in numerous ways, Bala said the city continues to offer much to explore. He described it as a place shaped by “thousands of years of lived experiences nourished by the Ganga”.
Director of Photography Marc Koninckx said his primary focus was to “catch emotions” on the actors’ faces through the use of light, camera angles, framing and composition. His aim, he said, was to make audiences feel part of the film rather than remain external observers.
“The camera is like music,” he said, explaining how he creates visual rhythm by juxtaposing colours and visual elements. He also observed that “too much colour kills colour”, highlighting the importance of using colours selectively to direct the audience’s attention and evoke emotions. This approach was particularly important while filming live at the Kumbh.
Actor Neeraj Kabi reflected on the lasting impact of the characters he portrays, saying that they often seep into his real life and become a part of him. His character in Banaras lives with dementia. Playing the role, he said, brought his own childhood to mind, a state in which the future does not exist and the present is absent.
Actor Abhishek Banerjee spoke about the challenges and spontaneity of shooting live at the Maha Kumbh, in contrast to working on controlled studio sets. Performing amid large crowds involved considerable uncertainty, he said, making the trust between the actor and director especially important. The experience took him back to his college days of performing nukkad nataks. Describing the shoot as “street cinema”, he said it transformed him both as an actor and as a person.
Rahman expressed his delight that two films featuring his music, Banaras and Ramayan, are being screened at the 57th IFFI rflecting the festival's celebration of diverse cinematic narratives and the enduring contribution of music to India's storytelling traditions.
The session was moderated by Shri Mahesh Kumar.

title: BRICS Film Festival Roundtable Explores Opportunities in Co-production, Distribution and Technology Exchange at 57th IFFI
subtitle: Representatives from participating countries highlight cinema's role in strengthening cultural ties and fostering mutual understanding
content:
Goa, 22 November 2026
Cinema may speak in different languages, but its emotions travel across borders. Bringing this shared language into focus, the BRICS Film Festival Roundtable at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) explored opportunities for greater collaboration among member countries, with discussions centred on co-production, film distribution, technology exchange and cultural partnerships.
The roundtable brought together representatives from Russia, Nigeria, Indonesia and Iran, along with officials from the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Ministry of External Affairs, National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) and Entertainment Society of Goa (ESG).
Additional Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Shri Prabhat, highlighted India’s commitment to strengthening cooperation among BRICS countries through shared interests and lasting partnerships. Observing that cinema brings people together and offers insights into different societies, he said the diverse genres and subjects represented through films help audiences discover new perspectives.
He also referred to India’s hosting of the BRICS WAVES Bazaar in Mumbai, where discussions covered international co-productions, artificial intelligence, animation, gaming and women’s leadership. Highlighting the growing interest in working together, he pointed to opportunities for identifying production partners across participating countries. He called for stronger co-production initiatives and greater exchange of content through digital television and OTT platforms, urging participants to build on the momentum for sustained partnerships.
Shri Shambhu L. Hakki, Joint Secretary, Ministry of External Affairs, said the gathering provided an opportunity to witness the BRICS partnership through cultural engagement. He emphasised that cinema is not merely a reflection of a nation but also a means of understanding one another. Referring to IFFI’s theme, Stories Without Borders, he noted that films from BRICS countries offer glimpses into the cultural expressions of partner nations, fostering understanding beyond institutional cooperation.
Chairman of NFDC Shri G. Krishnakumar highlighted the BRICS WAVES Bazaar held in Mumbai as an initiative that laid the foundation for bringing together filmmakers and industry stakeholders from BRICS countries. He emphasised the potential of film co-production in strengthening these connections and creating opportunities for collaborative storytelling.
Shri Dipak Bandekar, CEO of the Entertainment Society of Goa, described Goa as a meeting point for cinema and cultural exchange. He observed that while films may travel internationally, the emotions they convey are universal, making cinema a powerful medium for audiences to understand the cultures and experiences of other countries.
Representatives from participating countries also outlined possibilities for collaboration. H.E. Saidu Dahiru Muhammad, High Commissioner of the Federal Republic of Nigeria to India, spoke about the country’s vibrant film industry and welcomed the inclusion of Nigerian cinema in the festival. He identified co-production and distribution as promising areas of cooperation, alongside technology transfer and capacity building, which could create economic opportunities for younger generations.
Acting Consul General of the Consulate General of the Russian Federation in Mumbai Mr. Aleksandr Fursov highlighted cinema’s ability to transcend borders and referred to film festival exchanges between India and Russia as opportunities to deepen cultural connections.
First Secretary from the Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia in India, Ms. Erny Wahyuni spoke about the longstanding cultural links between India and Indonesia, reflected in shared traditions surrounding the Ramayana and Mahabharata. She proposed a familiarisation visit for filmmakers and producers as a step towards exploring co-production opportunities, alongside greater film distribution through OTT platforms. She also identified animation and gaming as areas with potential for collaboration and expressed interest in bringing cultural representatives, producers and animation professionals into future engagements.
Dr. Mostafa Goharifar, Deputy Chief of Mission, Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in India described Goa’s cultural diversity as an appropriate setting for conversations on understanding different societies. He observed that cinema offers a distinctive insight into nations and their people, and expressed hope that the gathering would lead to wider cooperation among film industries and communities.
In his concluding remarks, Shri G. Krishnakumar reiterated cinema’s role as a platform for bringing countries and cultures together. He thanked Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi and Union Minister Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw for their support, observing that collective efforts could create significant possibilities through cinema.
The roundtable concluded with a screening of a short video introducing the films from BRICS countries being showcased during the BRICS Film Festival, celebrating the diversity of their cinematic traditions.

title: ‘Ruby-Cube’ Explores the Complexities of Human Relationships and the Indian Family System: Director P. Sheshadri Interacts with Media at 57th IFFI
content:
Goa, 22 November 2026
The team of Kannada feature film Ruby-Cube interacted with the media at a press conference held on the sidelines of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Panaji, Goa, today. The interaction featured acclaimed filmmaker and Director P. Sheshadri and lead actor Vainidhi Jagadish.
Sharing his approach to filmmaking, P. Sheshadri said that he does not actively pursue stories but allows them to come to him. He explained that he makes a film only when a story genuinely appeals to him and he feels compelled to bring it to the screen. Describing Ruby-Cube as his 13th feature film, he said the narrative is rooted in real-life experiences and draws from the complexities of the Indian family system and the way relationships evolve within it.
The Director explained that the film explores several human issues and challenges through the lives of its characters. Comparing life to a Rubik’s Cube, he said that just as the puzzle has multiple colours and combinations, human lives too have different shades and dimensions. He emphasised that his films are not necessarily intended to deliver a specific message but to establish an emotional connection with audiences. He observed that IFFI provides an important platform for films to reach wider audiences, gain visibility and receive meaningful responses from cinema lovers.
Lead actor Vainidhi Jagadish spoke about the emotional layers of her character and the film's central premise, which revolves around a daughter returning to her parental home and gradually witnessing the dynamics of her parents' relationship. She highlighted how the film reflects contemporary family realities, where individuals often lead different lives while navigating changing relationships, expectations and emotional challenges. Describing about the film she said that the story is subtle and understated, focusing on everyday human experiences rather than dramatic expressions.
Set against the backdrop of a short vacation in a hill station, Ruby-Cube brings three generations of a family together under one roof. The story follows Rohini, a psychologist, who reunites with her former husband Moorthy when their daughter Chitra brings them together while dealing with challenges in her own marriage. As the family spends time together, unresolved emotions, old relationships and questions of responsibility gradually surface.
The interaction at IFFI 2026 offered audiences and the media an insight into the creative vision behind Ruby-Cube and its exploration of contemporary family relationships. The film's screening at the festival adds to IFFI's celebration of diverse cinematic voices and storytelling traditions across borders.

title: Who Says Only Boys Can Roar Like Tigers? Baghuni Tells the Story of a Young Girl Challenging Gender Barriers in Traditional Tiger Dance
subtitle: The Odia film celebrates courage, cultural identity and the freedom to pursue one's dreams
content:
Goa, 21 November 2026
What if a little girl decided that some traditions were meant to be danced with, not simply followed? What if she dared to enter a world where the tiger's stripes were traditionally painted on men and asked, “Why not me?”
This is the story of Mini, an 11-year-old girl from a remote village in Odisha, who dreams of becoming a
Bagha Nacha
performer. A traditional tiger dance form long dominated by men, Bagha Nacha is a cultural practice that Mini wishes to embrace on her own terms. For her, the aspiration is not merely about performing a dance, but about having the freedom to dream, challenge conventions and pursue her passion.
Inspired by true events,
Baghuni
(Dance Like a Tiger), written and directed by National Award-winning filmmaker Jitendra Mishra, tells the story of a young girl's determination to challenge deep-rooted gender stereotypes. Set against the backdrop of Odisha's vibrant folk traditions, the film explores gender barriers, social conditioning, cultural identity and the courage to question established norms. The film held its gala premiere at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa on November 22, 2026.
Addressing the press conference, Jitendra Mishra described
Baghuni
as a deeply personal milestone, marking his directorial debut after nearly two decades in the film industry. Recalling his association with IFFI's Indian Panorama over the years, he expressed gratitude to IFFI, NFDC and the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting for their support.
Speaking about the film, Mishra said that while Bagha Nacha provides its cultural backdrop, the story ultimately celebrates gender equality, courage and the human spirit. Inspired by the seven remarkable women in his own family, he emphasised that girls, when given equal opportunities, can excel beyond expectations. Rooted in extensive research in Berhampur, Odisha, the film also features local children selected through auditions across the state and trained for several months alongside seasoned actor Sabyasachi Mishra.
Acclaimed Odia actor Sabyasachi Mishra described
Baghuni
as a refreshing blend of compelling storytelling and Odisha's rich cultural heritage. He highlighted the contrast between Bagha Nacha, the traditional tiger dance, and Baghuni, meaning tigress, as central to the narrative, adding depth and intrigue to the film.
Sharing his experience of portraying a traditional Bagha Nacha performer, Sabyasachi revealed that he shed 30 kilograms and underwent rigorous physical and spiritual preparation to bring authenticity to the role. He also spoke about the demanding rituals and hours of intricate body painting associated with the folk art, in which the performer is revered as an embodiment of Goddess Maa Bhagabati Budhi Thakurani. Expressing confidence in the film's global appeal, he said
Baghuni
has the potential to set a new benchmark for regional Odia cinema and urged the media to take its message to audiences worldwide.
Producer Partha Panda expressed gratitude to IFFI, NFDC and the Government of India for honouring
Baghuni
with a gala premiere and providing a platform to showcase Odisha's cultural heritage to an international audience.
Through Mini's journey, Baghuni brings a deeply rooted local tradition into a larger aqnd more global conversation about courage, identity and the freedom to challenge convention. In this spirit, the film resonates with the theme of IFFI 2026, 'Stories Without Borders', reaffirming how cinema can carry local voices to global audiences and make stories from one corner of the world meaningful to another.
